A Massachusetts coastal zone mapping record from 2008 says the Hubline is about 29.5 miles, built mostly offshore between Beverly and Weymouth, as-built and in operation since November 2003 (per the queue note). ANGDA Glennallen to Palmer Spur Line

The Alaska Natural Gas Development Authority filed a right-of-way lease application dated April 4, 2005 with the State of Alaska for a buried 24-inch steel gas pipeline of about 148 miles from Glennallen to just west of Palmer, with a stated capacity of 1,000 million standard cubic feet per day. The application is the concrete step. The sponsor is a State of Alaska public corporation. Search results from the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas show a native lands report supporting a conditional right-of-way lease application, and a Petroleum News piece from September 2006 discusses the spur line, but neither was read for the length. A later Alaska Division of Oil and Gas summary calls it 143 miles; the application itself says 148. No sign of construction, a start year, or activity after about 2008 was found, so the status shelved with type inferred is a presumption and no URL backs it. Status needs a check by a person. The applicant is not in the owner list; the entity lookup found no exact match and the style tool found no legal form. Route not found, so no route is proposed. Only one source states the values, so the tier is medium. Extra context pages that load: https://dog.dnr.alaska.gov/Documents/SPCS/ANGDA/FinalReports/MiscellaneousReports/NativeLandReport.pdf and https://www.petroleumnews.com/pntruncate/28843979.shtml. The start location was recorded from the application text, which says the line begins in Glennallen on Ahtna lands.

Concrete step: ANR entered FERC pre-filing on March 12, 2026 (docket PF26-6); formal application planned October 2026, certificate October 2027, in service November 1, 2029. The TC Energy project page states about 92 miles, Michigan and Wisconsin, 2029, and about 0.4 Bcf/d. TC Energy page and EIA table both trace to the operator, so they count as one origin and the tier is medium. The 36 inch diameter is stated only in the EIA table. Atmos Energy and Energy Transfer Partners announced a letter of intent in December 2005 for a 45 mile, 30 inch intrastate line from Atmos Line W near Justin to near Frisco, Texas, in service by end of 2006, 200,000 MMBtu/d initial. The Natural Gas Intelligence pieces (p=53016 and p=24465) are one wire story, so one origin. The EIA August 2026 release, sheet Historical Projects, Excel rows 360 (West Side, 22 mi, completed May 2005 per EIA) and 407 (East Side, 25 mi, completed October 2006), lists both halves as completed new 30 inch intrastate pipe by Atmos Energy Inc, 225 MMcf/d each, total 47 mi. Length staged as the EIA 47 mi total; the announcement said 45 mi. Capacity 225 MMcf/d is EIA's per-half figure for the same line, not additive. Start year 2006 uses the later (East Side) completion date. Ownership: the announcement named Energy Transfer Partners as a joint owner funding the initial capital, but EIA lists Atmos as operator and the final split was not found; only Atmos staged. Only the 5,700 mi parent system P0369 exists in GEM, so this is a new expansion-style row under the same pipeline name. Not verified against the Texas Railroad Commission T-4 permit. No route researched. Tier medium: one origin each for announcement and EIA, completion not confirmed by an operator source.

Gas pipeline in North Dakota. WBI Energy Transmission proposes about 374 miles from near Watford City to its compressor station near Mapleton, built in two phases. The company project page says the length is about 374 miles after a binding open season in March 2026 and gives FERC pre-filing docket PF26-4. The EIA August 2026 release, Natural Gas Pipeline Projects sheet, Excel row 12, lists 350 miles, 1,000 million cubic feet per day, 36 or 42 inch for phase 1 and 24, 30 or 36 inch for phase 2, status pre-applied, in service 2029. The later 374 mile figure is used. Oil and Gas Watch (May 13, 2026) reports 374 miles, 1 billion cubic feet per day, state financing of up to 500 million dollars confirmed April 29, 2026, FERC scoping meetings, phase 1 in November 2029 and phase 2 in November 2030. FERC issued a notice of scoping in May 2026 per EIA. Concrete step met: FERC pre-filing, binding open season, state financing. Not an existing row. The Brazoria Interconnector Gas Pipeline is an existing 42 inch gas line in Brazoria County, Texas. A World Pipelines article from January 2015 says it runs 30.5 miles from Stratton Ridge in the south to a point near Iowa Colony in the north. It is not the 10.6 mile Freeport LNG Train 4 feed line (existing row P3666) and not the 0.5 mile Stratton Ridge row (P1297). A 2019 federal order on the Freeport LNG Train 4 project lists the Brazoria Interconnector Pipeline as one of the lines that feeds the Stratton Ridge Meter Station, separately from the new 10.6 mile line. The Energy Information Administration project table for August 2026 (sheet Historical Projects, Excel row 497) lists it as a completed 2008 intrastate expansion in Texas, 30 miles, 42 inches, with 2,600 million cubic feet per day of added capacity. The consolidator note says it runs to Freeport LNG, but the source says it ends near Iowa Colony, so the endpoint follows the source. Start year 2008 comes only from the EIA table (April 2008 in service date). It is intrastate, so no federal filing is expected. Owner left blank on purpose. ConocoPhillips owned it. The EIA table names Freeport LNG Development LP, which conflicts. Capacity left blank because the sources give 1.8 billion cubic feet per day (2015 article) and 2,600 million cubic feet per day (EIA), they disagree, and the sheet has no billion cubic feet per day unit. The route was not researched. Length of 30.5 miles is above the 15.5 mile threshold. The 2019 federal order was checked for the pipeline name only and is cited in no field. Canyon Gas; Kaskida gas export line
Tie-in to Magnolia Gas Gathering Pipeline

Enbridge press release of 3 October 2024 says it sanctioned and will build, own and operate the Canyon Gathering System, a 12 inch, 125 million cubic feet per day gas line for the bp Kaskida field. It connects subsea to Enbridge's existing Magnolia Gas Gathering Pipeline, which feeds Garden Banks Gas Pipeline. Expected in service by 2029. Offshore Magazine, reporting Enbridge, gives about 60 miles of pipe, starting at Keathley Canyon Block 293 in about 5,900 feet of water, growing to about 115 miles if bp exercises its options. The 195 km in the consolidator note does not match: 60 miles is about 97 km, and 195 km is close to the 115 mile option case or the oil line, so the 60 mile figure is staged. Cost of about 700 million US dollars covers the oil and gas lines together, so no cost is staged. This is a gathering line, and PipelineType gathering is in the GEM vocabulary. It is not the Magnolia Intrastate Pipeline (P0294, Louisiana onshore) or P2559 Magnolia Gas Pipeline, which are different systems. No existing row found for Canyon. Both sources trace to the same Enbridge announcement, so not independent; tier medium. Status proposed because construction has not started, with FID reached. No public route found, so route is unavailable. Exact end tie-in location not stated. Parent company named by the sources: Enbridge Inc.

Intrastate North Carolina gas line, in service since 1999, with no row in the roster. It is not Carolina Gas Transmission (P3221, P4381) and not the Mountain Valley Southgate row. A Cardinal Pipeline Company press release from March 2010 says the line is 105 miles and 24 inches, runs from Rockingham County to a point southeast of Raleigh, and has a design capacity of about 279,000 dekatherms per day. Its members are subsidiaries of Williams Partners, PSNC Energy and Piedmont, and it takes gas from an interconnect with Transco. The EIA pipeline projects table for August 2026 (sheet Historical Projects, Excel row 128, project name Cardinal Pipeline, operator Transcontinental Gas Pipeline) lists a completed new pipeline, 67 miles, 24 inches, 263 MMcf/d, cost 98.3 million dollars, in service November 1999, intrastate, state authority. Length conflict: 67 miles in EIA versus 105 miles from the operator. The staged value is 105 miles because the operator states it directly and it is the later figure, which likely includes later extensions. The 67 mile figure is the original 1999 build. Either is far above the 25 km threshold. The two sources are not fully independent on length because they disagree. Capacity unit is Dekatherms per day as the source states. A 2012 expansion of 199,000 Dth/d was planned in the same release and is not staged. Owner is the operating company. Member shares are not stated, so Parent is left blank. Capacity listed by EIA is 263 MMcf/d. No route found yet. Route research is still owed: check the North Carolina Utilities Commission and the state pipeline safety records. Intrastate lines do not appear in FERC filings, so silence there is not a concern. The NGI and Pipeline and Gas Journal pages from the candidate list were not used as refs: the NGI page returned 403 and the Pipeline and Gas Journal article is behind a paywall. Treated as one row. Length staged as 232 mi, the phase 1 plus phase 3 pipe, because the 32-mile phase 2 looks like the Carthage Loop, which a May 2008 trade press report says was completed in 2008 on the same line from Minden to Carthage; the EIA total of 264 mi and Energy Transfer's own 243 mile figure (from a March 2007 company release seen only in search results, the company site blocks automated fetches, so it is not cited) do not agree, so length is uncertain by about 10 percent. A June 2006 press report says the planned 42-inch Cleburne to Carthage line would cost $535 million and carry 1.6 Bcf/d, with XTO signed for 200 MMcf/d. If the Carthage Loop is ruled its own row, it is 32 mi of 42-inch pipe (51 km, over the 25 km threshold) and would need a separate shard. Confidence medium: EIA is one origin, press reports corroborate the project but not the length. [QC] independent=yes claimed on 9 surviving ref(s) from 0 publisher(s) -> no.
